explanation:
The standard C++ `typeid` operator, combined with the `name` member of the `type_info` class it returns, provides a built-in mechanism for runtime type identification. However, for the purpose of accurately viewing deduced types in templates or with `auto`, this tool is fundamentally misleading because its behavior is specified to mimic pass-by-value semantics.

Scott Meyers' crucial insight is that the C++ standard mandates `type_info::name` to treat the type as if it were a by-value function parameter. This means the type undergoes 'decay' before its name is reported. This decay process strips away the very details—references and top-level cv-qualifiers—that are often the subject of debugging in modern C++ generic code.

The mechanics of this decay are identical to the template type deduction rules for value parameters. First, if the type is a reference, its reference-ness is completely ignored. Second, after the reference is stripped, any top-level `const` or `volatile` qualifiers on the resulting type are also removed. For example, if you inspect a parameter of type `const int&`, `typeid` will first strip the reference to get `const int`, and since the `const` is top-level, it will also be stripped, resulting in a reported type of `int`.

This behavior has severe practical implications for debugging. When working with universal (forwarding) references, `typeid` will not show whether the argument was an lvalue or an rvalue, as it discards the reference qualifier that holds this information. Similarly, it can hide whether a deduced type is `const`, leading to confusion about why certain operations are or are not permitted on a template parameter. It provides a false sense of security and can send developers down the wrong path when diagnosing type-related issues.

The most common pitfall is simply trusting the output of `typeid(...).name()` to be the literal, exact type of an expression. Programmers are often surprised to see references and `const` qualifiers disappear from the output, leading to an incorrect mental model of what the compiler has actually deduced.
practical_example: When debugging a factory function that uses perfect forwarding, a developer might use `typeid` to check the type of a forwarded argument. If an lvalue `const Widget` is passed, `typeid` would likely report just `Widget`, hiding both the `const` and the lvalue reference nature of the argument, making it impossible to diagnose why a non-`const` method call is failing inside the factory.
keywords: typeid auto, typeid removes reference, typeid deduction issues, typeid pass-by-value
chapter: Item 4: Know how to view deduced types
book: Effective Modern C++ by Scott Meyers
